Public Healthcare Facilities in Cuttack District, Odisha
A Structured Reference Guide to District, Community, and Primary Health Facilities
Overview
Cuttack district is one of Odisha's most populous and historically significant districts, and its headquarters town, Cuttack city, has long served as a major medical hub for the wider region — it hosts the SCB Medical College and Hospital, one of the oldest and largest tertiary-care government teaching hospitals in eastern India.

Below this tertiary tier, the district's public healthcare network follows the same tiered structure used across India: village-level Sub-Centres feed into Primary Health Centres (PHCs), which refer upward to Community Health Centres (CHCs), which in turn refer to the District Headquarters Hospital (DHH) as the district's secondary-level referral point. This structure is coordinated locally by the Chief District Medical Officer (CDMO), Cuttack, under the Odisha Department of Health & Family Welfare, and follows standards set nationally through the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) via the National Health Mission (NHM), most recently revised in 2022.

Facility Types
District Headquarters Hospital (DHH), Cuttack
The DHH functions as the district's main secondary-level referral hospital, distinct from the tertiary-care SCB Medical College and Hospital located in the same city. It is intended to receive cases referred from CHCs, PHCs, and Sub-Centres across Cuttack district's blocks, and to provide a broader range of inpatient, diagnostic, and specialist services than block-level facilities. The exact current designation, address, and administrative details of the DHH should be confirmed with the CDMO Cuttack office, as this document does not independently verify facility-specific particulars.

Community Health Centres (CHCs)
CHCs are block-level referral units, generally built to serve a population of roughly 80,000 to 120,000 people, with lower population norms in hilly or tribal areas. Cuttack district's blocks (such as Athagarh, Banki, Salepur, Niali, Tangi-Choudwar, and others) are each expected to have a CHC serving as the referral point for PHCs within that block. A CHC is designed to have around 30 inpatient beds, an operation theatre, basic diagnostic and blood storage facilities, and specialist coverage in areas such as medicine, surgery, obstetrics/gynaecology, and paediatrics, though actual staffing and equipment levels vary by centre. Centres equipped for round-the-clock emergency obstetric and newborn care may additionally be designated First Referral Units (FRUs).

Primary Health Centres (PHCs)
PHCs are typically the first point of contact with a qualified doctor for rural and semi-urban residents, each covering a population of around 20,000 to 30,000. A PHC supervises a cluster of Sub-Centres in its area and is expected to provide outpatient consultation, a small number of inpatient beds (around four to six), basic laboratory testing, and normal delivery services at PHCs designated for 24x7 care. PHCs also oversee ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) and ANM (Auxiliary Nurse Midwife) workers operating at the village level. Sub-Centres and Health & Wellness Centres
The most peripheral public health facilities are Health Sub-Centres, increasingly being upgraded as Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs).

These are generally staffed by an ANM and a Community Health Officer and focus on preventive and promotive care — immunization, antenatal check-ups, and basic screening — referring more complex cases upward to the PHC.

What Each Facility Handles
District Headquarters Hospital
Complex and emergency cases referred from CHCs and PHCs across the district
Broader specialist consultation and surgical services than block-level facilities
Diagnostics, blood storage/blood bank services, and larger inpatient bed capacity
Possible empanelment under schemes such as Ayushman Bharat–PM-JAY for cashless treatment (current empanelment status should be verified locally)
Acts as the secondary-level referral hospital for the district, with onward referral to SCB Medical College and Hospital or another tertiary centre for cases needing higher-level specialty or super-specialty care
Community Health Centres
Referral care for PHCs within the block, plus specialist consultation for patients approaching directly
Inpatient care (around 30 beds), minor and some major surgical procedures, and operation theatre services
Emergency obstetric care and institutional deliveries, particularly at centres designated as First Referral Units
Basic diagnostics including laboratory services and, at many centres, X-ray facilities
Primary Health Centres
Outpatient consultation for common illnesses, minor injuries, and chronic disease follow-up
Antenatal, natal, and postnatal care, including normal deliveries at 24x7 PHCs
Immunization, family planning services, and national health programme delivery (TB, malaria, non-communicable disease screening, and similar)
Basic laboratory tests (blood, urine, blood sugar, malaria rapid tests, and similar)
First-level stabilization and referral of serious cases to a CHC or the District Headquarters Hospital
How to Reach Them (General Guidance)
Since exact addresses and phone numbers are not being invented here, the following general approaches can help locate and reach the correct facility:
Ask the local ASHA worker, ANM, or Anganwadi worker — they know the nearest Sub-Centre and PHC serving a household and can help with referral upward if needed.

Every block headquarters in Cuttack district has a CHC; the block administrative (Block Development/Tahasil) office can confirm its exact location. The Cuttack district administration's official website and the CDMO Cuttack office maintain listings of health facilities; these should be treated as the authoritative source for confirmed addresses and phone numbers. The National Health Mission (NHM) Odisha and Odisha Directorate of Health Services websites publish facility directories and health scheme information at the state level. The 108 (emergency response) and 102 (patient transport / maternal-child) ambulance services can be used to reach an appropriate facility in an emergency, and can also help route a patient to the correct level of care.

For the District Headquarters Hospital specifically, and to distinguish it from SCB Medical College and Hospital in the same city, confirm the current address and scope of services with the district health administration before travelling.

When to Go to District Hospital vs PHC
Go to a PHC (or Sub-Centre) first for:
Routine illnesses — fever, cold, minor infections, common ailments
Antenatal check-ups, immunizations, and family planning services
Normal, uncomplicated deliveries at a 24x7-designated PHC
Basic diagnostic tests and follow-up for chronic conditions already under management
Minor injuries and first-aid level care
Go to (or be referred to) a CHC for:
Cases needing minor surgery, specialist consultation, or inpatient observation beyond what a PHC can provide
Complicated deliveries or emergency obstetric care, especially at an FRU-designated CHC
Situations where the PHC has stabilized a patient but recommended referral
Go directly to the District Headquarters Hospital for:
Serious emergencies — major trauma, accidents, severe medical emergencies where higher-level care is clearly needed
Conditions requiring specialist care, surgery, or diagnostics not available at PHC or CHC level
Cases already referred by a PHC or CHC as needing secondary-level hospital care
Situations covered under empanelled schemes (e.g., PM-JAY) requiring hospital-level admission — confirm current scheme coverage locally
As a general rule, the public health system is designed as a step-up referral chain: Sub-Centre → PHC → CHC → District Headquarters Hospital → Medical College Hospital, with each level equipped for progressively more complex care.

In Cuttack's case, the presence of SCB Medical College and Hospital in the same city as the DHH means very serious or specialized cases may ultimately be referred there, but the DHH and CHCs remain the intended first stops for most secondary-level care under the standard referral pathway. Bypassing lower tiers is appropriate mainly in genuine emergencies, where reaching the nearest capable facility quickly — often via 108 ambulance services — matters more than following the tier order.

Sources Used

The structural and functional information above is grounded in national IPHS/NHM/MoHFW standards, which apply uniformly across Odisha's districts. Dengue Fever: Public Health Awareness Guide
A simple reference for community health awareness (for use by health awareness chatbots and community health workers)
Overview
Dengue fever is an illness spread by the bite of an infected mosquito. It is caused by the dengue virus and is common in tropical and sub-tropical parts of the world, including most of India. Both children and adults can get dengue. Many people who get infected have no symptoms at all or only mild symptoms, and most people recover fully within one to two weeks with proper rest and care. In a small number of cases, dengue can become severe and needs urgent hospital treatment.

In a small number of cases, dengue can become severe and needs urgent hospital treatment. Because there is no specific medicine that cures dengue, the best protection is preventing mosquito bites and stopping mosquitoes from breeding around homes and villages. Common Symptoms
Dengue usually begins suddenly, about four to seven days after the mosquito bite. Common signs include:
Sudden high fever
Severe headache, often with pain behind the eyes
Muscle, joint, and body pain (sometimes called “break-bone fever”)
Nausea and vomiting
Skin rash, which may appear a few days after the fever starts
Weakness and loss of appetite
Mild bleeding, such as from the gums or nose, in some cases
Most people start feeling better after the fever comes down, usually within a week.

However, a few people can develop severe dengue just as the fever is going down, which is why it is important to keep watching for warning signs even after the fever reduces. Causes
Dengue is caused by the dengue virus, which spreads to people through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. These mosquitoes are most active during the day, especially in the early morning and before sunset. They breed in clean, standing water that collects in and around homes, such as in water storage containers, discarded tyres, flower pots, coolers, tanks, tins, and other containers that hold rainwater. Dengue does not spread directly from one person to another through touch, coughing, or sharing food; it spreads only through mosquito bites.

A person can get dengue more than once in their life, and a second infection can sometimes be more severe than the first. When to See a Doctor (Warning Signs – Act Immediately)
Most dengue cases can be managed at home with rest and fluids, but some warning signs mean the person needs urgent medical attention, ideally at a hospital or health centre.

Go to a doctor or hospital immediately if the person has any of the following:
Severe stomach pain or continuous vomiting
Bleeding from the nose, gums, or blood in vomit or stool (black stool)
Difficulty breathing or fast, shallow breathing
Extreme tiredness, restlessness, or confusion
Cold, clammy skin or pale skin
Not passing urine for several hours
Fever that suddenly drops but the person feels worse, not better
Any bleeding under the skin (small red or purple spots)
These warning signs often appear as the fever is coming down, usually three to seven days after symptoms start.

Infants, pregnant women, older adults, and people with other health conditions should be watched extra carefully and taken to a doctor early, even for mild symptoms, since they have a higher chance of complications.

Home Care and Prevention
Home care (for mild dengue without warning signs):
Rest as much as possible and avoid heavy physical activity
Drink plenty of fluids – water, oral rehydration solution (ORS), coconut water, or fruit juice – to prevent dehydration
Eat light, easily digestible food
Check body temperature regularly and watch for warning signs
Do not take any medicine without consulting a doctor, since some common painkillers can increase the risk of bleeding in dengue
Use a mosquito net or repellent while resting, so the patient does not spread infection to more mosquitoes, which can then bite others
Prevention (stopping mosquito breeding):
Empty, clean, or cover all containers that can collect water – buckets, drums, coolers, flower pots, and tanks – at least once a week
Remove stagnant water from around the house, including in tyres, broken pots, and construction sites
Keep drains clear and avoid letting water collect in open spaces
Use mosquito nets, screens on windows, and mosquito repellents, especially during the day
Wear clothes that cover arms and legs, particularly for children and during outdoor work
Support community and municipal efforts such as fogging and larvicide spraying, and report breeding sites to local health workers
Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, dengue follows a clear seasonal pattern linked to the state's monsoon and post-monsoon periods.

Cases typically begin rising with the arrival of the south-west monsoon around June to July and peak during the post-monsoon months of September to November, when heavy rainfall combined with warm, humid weather creates ideal breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes. Coastal and urban districts, including areas around Bhubaneswar, Cuttack, Khurda, and Jajpur, along with parts of southern and tribal-dominated districts, have historically reported higher case numbers during these months, though outbreaks can occur across most districts of the state. Because Odisha experiences heavy monsoon rainfall and frequent waterlogging, extra care is needed to prevent water from collecting in open drains, construction sites, discarded containers, tyres, and low-lying areas after rains.

Rural households should regularly check water storage pots, coolers, and any containers used for rainwater harvesting, since these become common breeding grounds once the rains begin. Community-level cleanliness drives, timely desilting of drains, and prompt reporting of fever cases to the nearest health centre or Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) worker can help control local outbreaks. Awareness and early action before and during the monsoon season are especially important in reducing the annual rise in dengue cases seen across the state.

Understanding Diabetes
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
Diabetes is a long-term health condition that affects how the body turns food into energy. Normally, the food we eat is broken down into sugar (glucose), which enters the blood. A hormone called insulin, made by the pancreas, helps this sugar move into the body's cells to be used for energy. In diabetes, the body either does not make enough insulin, or is unable to use the insulin it makes properly. As a result, sugar builds up in the blood instead of reaching the cells. Over time, this extra sugar in the blood can damage the heart, eyes, kidneys, nerves, and blood vessels.

Diabetes is one of the most common long-term health conditions in India today, affecting both cities and villages. It can affect adults and, increasingly, younger people as well. The good news is that with awareness, healthy habits, and regular check-ups, diabetes can often be prevented, or managed well if it does occur. Common Symptoms
Diabetes often develops slowly, and many people do not notice any symptoms in the early stages.

When symptoms do appear, they may include:
Feeling very thirsty often, even after drinking water
Passing urine more often than usual, including at night
Feeling unusually tired or weak
Losing weight without trying
Feeling hungry more often than normal
Blurred or unclear eyesight
Cuts, wounds, or sores that take longer than usual to heal
Frequent infections, such as skin or urinary infections
Tingling, numbness, or a burning feeling in the hands or feet
Because these symptoms can be mild at first, many people are not aware they have diabetes until it is checked through a simple blood test.

Causes
Diabetes can develop for several reasons, and often more than one factor is involved:
Family history – having parents or close relatives with diabetes increases risk
Being overweight or having extra fat around the stomach
Low levels of physical activity or a sedentary daily routine
Unhealthy eating habits, such as regularly eating a lot of sugar, refined (polished) grains, oily, or fried food
Increasing age, especially after 40 years
High blood pressure or high cholesterol
Diabetes that occurs during pregnancy (gestational diabetes), which can raise future risk for both mother and child
Long-term stress and irregular sleep patterns
In some cases, particularly in younger people, diabetes occurs because the body's immune system affects the pancreas directly.

This form is not linked to lifestyle and cannot currently be prevented, but it can still be managed well with proper medical care. When to See a Doctor
Anyone experiencing the common symptoms above should visit the nearest health centre or doctor for a simple blood sugar test.

In addition, the following signs need urgent medical attention and should never be ignored:
Severe weakness, confusion, difficulty staying awake, or fainting
Fast breathing, breathlessness, or a fruity smell in the breath
Repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down
Severe stomach pain
A wound, ulcer, or sore (especially on the foot) that is not healing, is swollen, or has pus
Sudden blurred vision or loss of vision
Chest pain, pressure, or discomfort
Numbness, weakness, or slurred speech on one side of the body
Signs of very low blood sugar in a known diabetic person, such as sudden sweating, shakiness, or dizziness that does not improve after eating something sweet
Diabetes discovered or suspected during pregnancy
If any of these red-flag signs appear, the person should be taken to the nearest hospital or Primary Health Centre (PHC) immediately.

Early action can prevent serious complications and save lives. Home Care and Prevention
Many cases of the common (type 2) form of diabetes can be prevented or delayed through simple, everyday lifestyle habits.

These same habits also help people already living with diabetes stay healthier:
Healthy Eating
Include more vegetables, leafy greens, whole grains (such as unpolished rice, ragi, or millets), and pulses in daily meals
Reduce sugar, sweets, cold drinks, and refined white rice or maida-based foods
Limit deep-fried and oily food; choose boiled, steamed, or lightly cooked options when possible
Eat meals at regular times and avoid skipping meals, especially breakfast
Drink plenty of plain water through the day
Staying Active
Aim for at least 30 minutes of walking or physical activity most days of the week
Simple daily activities like farm work, walking to the market, or household chores also help
Avoid sitting for very long periods without moving
Healthy Body Weight and Habits
Maintaining a healthy body weight lowers the risk of developing diabetes
Avoid tobacco (smoking or chewing) and limit alcohol, as both increase risk
Get adequate sleep and try to manage stress through rest, family support, or community activities
General Care Awareness
Get blood sugar checked regularly, especially after age 40 or if there is a family history of diabetes

Diarrhoea and Dehydration in Children
A Public Health Awareness Reference
For community health awareness use • Simple language for rural readers
Overview
Diarrhoea means passing loose or watery stools three or more times in a day. It is one of the most common illnesses in young children and is a leading cause of child sickness and death in many parts of India, including rural and tribal areas. The main danger from diarrhoea is not the loose motions themselves, but the loss of water and salts from the body, known as dehydration. Dehydration can become severe within hours, especially in small children and infants, and can be life-threatening if not treated in time.

The good news is that most cases of diarrhoea can be safely managed at home with simple fluids, continued feeding, and Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS), along with quick recognition of warning signs that need medical care. Common Symptoms
Diarrhoea and dehydration can show up in different ways.

Common Symptoms
Diarrhoea and dehydration can show up in different ways. Common signs include:
Frequent loose or watery stools
Stomach pain or cramps
Nausea or vomiting
Mild fever
Weakness or tiredness
Loss of appetite
Signs that the body is losing too much fluid (early dehydration) include:
Thirst, dry mouth, or dry lips
Fewer wet diapers, or passing less urine than usual
Dark yellow urine
Reduced activity, irritability, or crying without tears
Sunken eyes
In infants, a sunken soft spot on the top of the head
Causes
Diarrhoea in children is usually caused by infections that spread through unsafe water, unwashed hands, or contaminated food.

Common causes include:
Viral infections (such as rotavirus), which are the most common cause in young children
Bacterial infections from contaminated food or water
Parasites and worms, especially where sanitation is poor
Drinking unclean or unboiled water
Poor handwashing, especially before eating and after using the toilet
Unsafe food storage or spoiled food
Malnutrition, which makes children more vulnerable to infection and to severe dehydration
When to See a Doctor — Red Flag Signs
Most diarrhoea can be managed at home, but the caregiver should take the child to the nearest health centre, ASHA worker, or hospital immediately if any of the following are seen:
Blood in the stool
Repeated vomiting, unable to keep down fluids or ORS
Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, dry mouth, no tears, little or no urine for 6 hours or more
Child is unusually sleepy, difficult to wake, or unresponsive
High fever that does not settle
Diarrhoea continues for more than 2 days without improvement
Severe stomach pain
Signs of severe weakness, fits (convulsions), or the child cannot drink or breastfeed at all
Infant below 6 months of age with diarrhoea
Child is malnourished or has an existing serious illness
If any of these signs appear, do not wait — seek medical help immediately.

ORS should still be given on the way to the health facility, if the child is able to drink. Home Care and Prevention
Home care during diarrhoea
Give ORS after every loose stool to replace lost fluids and salts. Continue breastfeeding infants — do not stop breastfeeding during diarrhoea. Continue feeding the child age-appropriate food; do not withhold food. Small, frequent meals are best. Give plenty of clean fluids such as ORS, safe drinking water, and home fluids like rice water or diluted buttermilk. Let the child rest as needed. Wash hands with soap before feeding the child and after cleaning the child's stool. Do not give unnecessary medicines without consulting a health worker or doctor. Watch closely for the red-flag signs listed above.

If a ready-made ORS packet from a health centre or ASHA worker is available, always prefer that — just follow the instructions printed on the packet, mixing it with the exact amount of clean water stated. If a packet is not available, a simple home sugar-salt solution can be prepared:
Wash hands well with soap and clean water. Take 1 litre of clean drinking water (boiled and cooled, if the water source is not safe). Add 6 level teaspoons of sugar. Add half (1/2) a level teaspoon of salt. Stir well until the sugar and salt fully dissolve. Give small sips frequently using a clean cup or spoon — do not use a feeding bottle.

Give small sips frequently using a clean cup or spoon — do not use a feeding bottle. If the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and then continue giving small sips more slowly. Prepare a fresh solution every day; discard any solution left over after 24 hours. Use a toilet/latrine and avoid open defecation. Keep food covered and eat freshly cooked food; avoid stale or exposed food. Wash fruits and vegetables before eating. Ensure children complete their scheduled vaccinations, including the rotavirus vaccine given under the national immunisation programme. Keep the child's surroundings and drinking water storage containers clean. Understanding the Symptom: Diarrhoea
A general health awareness reference (not a diagnosis)
Symptom Overview
Diarrhoea means passing loose or watery stools more often than usual, generally three or more times in a day. It is not a disease by itself — it is a sign that the digestive system is reacting to something, such as an infection, unclean food or water, or another illness. Diarrhoea may last for a short time (a day or two) or may continue for longer. It can occur alone or together with other symptoms such as stomach cramps, vomiting, fever, or weakness. The main danger from diarrhoea is loss of body fluids and salts (dehydration), which can become serious, especially in young children, elderly people, and pregnant women, if not managed in time.

Possible Common Causes
Diarrhoea can happen for many different reasons. This list only describes possible everyday causes — it does not diagnose any illness. A doctor or health worker should be consulted to know the exact cause.

A doctor or health worker should be consulted to know the exact cause. Drinking contaminated or unsafe water
Eating stale, spoiled, or improperly cooked food
Infections of the gut caused by viruses, bacteria, or parasites
Poor hand hygiene or unclean food handling and storage
Food intolerance or sensitivity to certain foods
Side effect of certain medicines, including some antibiotics
Indigestion from overeating or eating unfamiliar or very oily food
Stress or anxiety, in some individuals
Ongoing digestive conditions that need long-term medical care
Self-Care Advice
If diarrhoea is mild and the person is otherwise alert and able to drink fluids, simple home care often helps:
Drink plenty of safe fluids — water, ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution), or clean home-made fluids — to replace what is lost
If ORS packets are available, mix as per the instructions on the packet and sip small amounts frequently through the day
If ORS is not available, a simple home fluid can be made using clean water with a little salt and sugar
Continue eating light, easily digestible food such as rice, khichdi, banana, curd, or toast — do not stop feeding, especially in children
For infants, continue breastfeeding; offer ORS in addition, in small sips
Avoid oily, spicy, or very sugary food and drinks until the stomach settles
Zinc supplements (available at government health centres for children) can help shorten a diarrhoea episode in children — take only as advised by a health worker
Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet, and keep drinking water covered and clean
Rest as much as possible
When to Seek Medical Attention
Please visit the nearest health centre, sub-centre, or hospital without delay if any of the following are noticed:
⚠ Loose stools continue for more than two days without improvement
⚠ Signs of dehydration: very little or no urine, dry mouth, sunken eyes, extreme thirst, or in infants, no tears when crying and a sunken soft spot on the head
⚠ Blood or mucus in the stool
⚠ High fever that does not settle
⚠ Repeated vomiting along with diarrhoea, making it hard to keep fluids down
⚠ Severe stomach pain
⚠ Confusion, unusual drowsiness, fainting, or difficulty waking up
⚠ Diarrhoea in a small child, elderly person, or pregnant woman that does not improve quickly
⚠ Several members of the same household or community falling ill with similar symptoms around the same time
These signs may point to a more serious condition and need to be checked by a qualified doctor or health worker as soon as possible.

Symptom: Dizziness
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Symptom Overview
Dizziness is a general term for feeling unsteady, light-headed, or like the surroundings are spinning. Some people feel like they may faint, others feel off-balance while standing or walking, and some feel a spinning sensation known as vertigo. Dizziness may last a few seconds, come and go, or continue for a longer time. It can happen suddenly while standing up, during physical activity, or without any clear trigger. Dizziness is a symptom, not a disease by itself. It can be caused by many different things, from mild and temporary reasons to conditions that need medical attention. This document does not identify which condition you may have.

This document does not identify which condition you may have. It only offers general, safe information to help you understand dizziness as a symptom and decide your next steps. Possible Common Causes
Dizziness can happen for many reasons. Some common and general possibilities include:
Dehydration or heat exposure: Not drinking enough water, sweating heavily, or spending long hours in strong heat can lower fluid and salt levels and cause dizziness. Low blood pressure: Standing up too quickly, especially after sitting or lying down, can briefly reduce blood flow to the brain and cause light-headedness. Low blood sugar: Skipping meals or going without food for long periods can cause weakness, shakiness, and dizziness.

Anaemia (low blood count): Ongoing tiredness and dizziness can happen when the body does not have enough healthy red blood cells, often linked to poor diet. Inner ear problems: Conditions affecting the inner ear's balance system can cause a spinning sensation (vertigo), sometimes with nausea. Motion sickness: Travel by road, boat, or on rough terrain can cause temporary dizziness and nausea in some people. Stress, anxiety, or poor sleep: Emotional strain, overwork, or lack of rest can sometimes bring on light-headedness. Side effects of medicines: Certain medicines, including those for blood pressure or sedation, can cause dizziness as a side effect. This list is general and not complete. It is not possible to know the exact cause of dizziness from a description alone.

It is not possible to know the exact cause of dizziness from a description alone. A trained health worker or doctor needs to examine and, where needed, test the person to understand the cause. Self-Care Advice
For mild, brief dizziness with no other worrying symptoms, the following general steps may help:
Sit or lie down immediately when you feel dizzy, to avoid a fall or injury. Rise slowly from sitting or lying down, rather than standing up suddenly. Drink water, ORS (oral rehydration solution), or a fluid with a pinch of salt and sugar, especially in hot weather or after sweating heavily. Rest in a cool, shaded, well-ventilated place if the dizziness may be linked to heat. Eat regular meals and avoid going for long hours without food.

Eat regular meals and avoid going for long hours without food. Avoid sudden head movements or quick changes in position until the dizziness passes. Avoid driving, climbing, operating machinery, or working near heights or fire while feeling dizzy. If dizziness is mild and passes within a few minutes with rest and fluids, continue to observe yourself over the next day for repeat episodes. When to Seek Medical Attention

Fainting or loss of consciousness, even briefly. Chest pain, pounding or irregular heartbeat, or difficulty breathing. Sudden weakness or numbness in the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side of the body.

Sudden weakness or numbness in the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side of the body. Slurred speech, confusion, difficulty understanding others, or trouble seeing. Severe headache that comes on suddenly and is unlike any headache before. Repeated vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down. A fall or head injury linked to the dizzy spell. Dizziness with high fever, severe dehydration, or signs of heat stroke, such as very hot skin, confusion, or not sweating despite heat. Dizziness that is severe, does not improve with rest, keeps returning, or is getting worse over time. Dizziness in a pregnant woman, elderly person, small child, or someone with a known heart condition, diabetes, or high blood pressure.

Elderly Health Awareness
Simple Steps for a Healthier, Safer Old Age
A Public Health Awareness Guide for Families and Communities
1. Overview
As people grow older, their bodies go through natural changes. Bones become weaker, eyesight and hearing may reduce, muscles lose strength, and the body takes longer to recover from illness. These changes are a normal part of ageing, but many problems linked to old age can be reduced or managed if families and elders themselves stay aware and take small precautions. India's elderly population is growing steadily every year. Health authorities have recognised that older adults need special attention because they often deal with more than one health condition at the same time, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, joint pain, or heart disease.

This guide explains, in simple language, the common health concerns of old age, how to prevent falls, and how to use medicines safely. It is meant for families in villages, small towns, and cities who want to care for their elders in the right way. 2. Key Practices
A. Common Age-Related Health Concerns
Joint and bone problems: Pain in knees, hips, and back is common due to weakening bones and joints. Regular gentle movement and a diet with calcium (milk, curd, green leafy vegetables) can help. High blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease: These are called non-communicable diseases and are very common in old age. Regular check-ups at the nearest sub-centre, PHC, or hospital help catch problems early. Weak eyesight and hearing: Cataracts and hearing loss increase with age.

Weak eyesight and hearing: Cataracts and hearing loss increase with age. Yearly eye and ear check-ups can prevent accidents and improve quality of life. Memory and mental health: Some elders may face memory loss, confusion, loneliness, or sadness. Family time, social activity, and talking openly about feelings are important. Weakness and poor nutrition: Loss of appetite and reduced ability to chew can lead to poor nutrition. Soft, nutritious, home-cooked food in small, frequent meals is helpful. B. Fall Prevention
Falls are one of the most common and serious risks for elderly people. A fall that seems minor can lead to a fracture, especially of the hip, and a long recovery. Most falls happen at home and can be prevented with simple changes.

Most falls happen at home and can be prevented with simple changes. Keep floors dry, clean, and free of loose wires, mats, or clutter, especially near the bathroom and stairs. Ensure good lighting in rooms, staircases, and passages, particularly at night. Fix strong handrails in bathrooms and along staircases; use a non-slip mat in the bathing area. Encourage the use of a walking stick or support if the elder feels unsteady while walking. Ask elders to rise slowly from sitting or lying down, as sudden movement can cause dizziness. Get eyesight, footwear, and blood pressure checked regularly, since poor vision, loose slippers, and low blood pressure are common causes of falls. C.

C. General Medication Safety Awareness
Older adults often take medicines for more than one condition, which increases the chance of mistakes or side effects. The following general practices support safe use of medicines, without replacing a doctor's or pharmacist's advice. Always take medicines exactly as prescribed by a qualified doctor; never start, stop, or change a dose on your own. Keep a simple written list or a medicine box with day and time markings to avoid missing or repeating a dose. Inform every doctor about all the medicines the elder is already taking, including any bought without prescription. Store medicines safely, away from direct sunlight and out of reach of children, and check expiry dates regularly.

Report any unusual symptoms after starting a new medicine, such as dizziness, drowsiness, or stomach upset, to a health worker or doctor promptly. Avoid sharing medicines between family members, as the same symptom can have different causes and treatments. 3. Why It Matters

A fall that leads to a hip fracture, or a medicine taken incorrectly, can turn a healthy elder into someone dependent on others for months. On the other hand, regular check-ups, a safe home environment, and careful use of medicines allow elders to stay active, independent, and mentally well for longer. Caring for elderly family members is also a shared social responsibility.

First Aid for Electric Shock
Immediate Response Before Medical Help Arrives
An electric shock happens when the body comes into contact with a live source of electrical current, such as faulty wiring, a damaged appliance, or a power line. The danger depends on the voltage, the current's path through the body, and how quickly help is given. Damage may not always be visible on the skin, since an electric current can injure the heart, muscles, and internal organs even when there is no obvious burn. Every electric shock, however minor it seems, deserves caution and medical evaluation. What to Do Immediately
1. Do not touch the person if they are still in contact with the electrical source. Touching them directly could pass the current through you as well. 2.

Touching them directly could pass the current through you as well. 2. Turn off the power at the source if possible, such as the switch, circuit breaker, or fuse box, before approaching the person. 3. If the power cannot be turned off, separate the person from the source using a dry, non-conducting object such as a wooden stick, plastic broom handle, or thick dry rope. Stand on a dry surface such as a wooden board, rubber mat, or stack of dry newspapers while doing this. 4. Once the person is safely away from the electrical source, check whether they are conscious and breathing. Call out to them and gently check for a response. 5.

Call out to them and gently check for a response. 5. If the person is not breathing or shows no signs of movement, coughing, or response, begin CPR immediately if you are trained, and continue until help arrives or the person recovers. 6. If the person is breathing but unconscious, place them in the recovery position (on their side) to keep the airway clear, and continue monitoring them. 7. Cover any visible burns loosely with a clean, dry, sterile dressing or cloth. Do not use a fluffy towel or blanket directly on a burn, since loose fibers can stick to the wound. 8. Keep the person warm and as still as possible, and continue watching their breathing, pulse, and responsiveness closely until emergency responders arrive.

What NOT to Do
• Do not touch the person while they are still in contact with the electrical current, even to try to help them; you risk being shocked yourself. • Do not use any metal, wet material, or damp cloth to move the person or the electrical source away, as these conduct electricity. • Do not approach downed power lines or high-voltage wires under any circumstances; stay well back and wait for the power company or emergency services to confirm the power is off. • Do not move the person unnecessarily unless they are in immediate danger, such as fire or ongoing electrical contact. • Do not pour water, apply ointments, ice, or butter to an electrical burn.

• Do not pour water, apply ointments, ice, or butter to an electrical burn. • Do not assume the person is fine just because there is no visible burn or they seem alert; internal damage, including to the heart, may not show right away. • Do not give the person food or water, in case medical treatment or anesthesia is needed soon after. • Do not delay calling for emergency help while attempting first aid; if you are alone, call for help as soon as the person is safely away from the current, or as you begin care if a phone is nearby. When to Call Emergency Services
Call an ambulance (108 in India, or the local emergency number) immediately if any of the following apply:
• The person has lost consciousness, is not breathing normally, or shows no signs of circulation.

• The shock came from a high-voltage source, a power line, or lightning. • There are visible burns, especially if they appear deep, widespread, or are on the face, hands, feet, or genitals. • The person has chest pain, an irregular heartbeat, difficulty breathing, or seizures. • The person appears confused, disoriented, or has persistent muscle pain, numbness, or weakness. • The shock passed through the chest, or you are unsure how severe the current or exposure was. • Any electric shock has occurred in a child, elderly person, or pregnant woman, since even a seemingly mild shock warrants prompt medical review. • You are unsure whether the shock was serious, since even a shock that looks minor can cause hidden internal or cardiac injury that needs medical evaluation.

Go straight to the nearest hospital or emergency room, or call your local emergency ambulance number right away. Why This Matters
For certain symptoms, every minute counts. Conditions such as heart attack, stroke, severe bleeding, and meningitis can worsen very quickly, and the treatments that work best are often only effective if given early.

Waiting to "see if it gets better" can mean the difference between a full recovery and permanent damage, or between life and death. This guide is intentionally cautious: if a symptom is on this list, treat it as an emergency, even if the person seems to be coping or the symptom seems to be easing. Warning Signs That Need Immediate Care
1. Chest Pain or Pressure
Chest pain, tightness, pressure, or a squeezing sensation, especially if it spreads to the arm, jaw, neck, or back, or comes with sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath, can be a sign of a heart attack. Heart muscle can be permanently damaged within a short time if blood flow is blocked, so rapid treatment significantly improves the chance of survival and recovery.

Act now: Call emergency services or go to the nearest hospital immediately. Do not drive yourself if possible; do not wait to see if the pain passes. 2. Difficulty Breathing or Severe Shortness of Breath
Struggling to breathe, breathlessness that does not improve with rest, gasping for air, or lips or fingertips turning blue or grey are signs that the body is not getting enough oxygen. This can be caused by a severe asthma attack, a serious infection, a heart problem, a blocked airway, or a severe allergic reaction, all of which can become life-threatening within minutes. Act now: Call emergency services or go to the nearest hospital immediately. Sit the person upright if possible and loosen tight clothing while help is on the way. 3.

Sit the person upright if possible and loosen tight clothing while help is on the way. 3. Severe Bleeding
Bleeding that will not stop after applying firm, direct pressure for several minutes, bleeding that is spurting or gushing, or a large, deep wound can quickly lead to dangerous blood loss and shock. This includes severe bleeding after an accident, a deep cut, or heavy bleeding during or after pregnancy. Act now: Apply firm, continuous pressure with a clean cloth and call emergency services or get to the nearest hospital immediately. Do not remove an object stuck in a wound; keep pressure around it instead. 4.

Do not remove an object stuck in a wound; keep pressure around it instead. 4. Sudden Weakness, Numbness, or Signs of Stroke
Sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body, a drooping face, slurred or confused speech, sudden vision problems, sudden severe headache, or loss of balance can be signs of a stroke. Brain cells begin to die within minutes when blood flow is interrupted, and treatments that can limit damage generally only work if given very soon after symptoms start. A simple way to check is the FAST test: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call for help. Act now: Call emergency services or get to the nearest hospital immediately, even if the symptoms seem to improve or come and go. Note the time the symptoms started, as this helps doctors decide on treatment. 5.

Note the time the symptoms started, as this helps doctors decide on treatment. 5. High Fever With a Stiff Neck
A high fever combined with a stiff neck, severe headache, sensitivity to light, confusion, or a rash that does not fade when pressed can be signs of meningitis or a similar severe infection affecting the brain and spinal cord. This condition can worsen very rapidly and can be fatal or cause lasting harm without urgent treatment, particularly in young children, older adults, and people with weaker immune systems. Act now: Go to the nearest hospital or call emergency services immediately. Do not wait to see if the fever comes down on its own. 6.

Do not wait to see if the fever comes down on its own. 6. Severe Abdominal Pain
Sudden, severe, or worsening pain in the abdomen, especially if it is constant, focused in one area, or comes with vomiting, fever, a rigid or very tender belly, or blood in vomit or stool, can indicate a serious internal problem such as appendicitis, a perforated organ, a blocked intestine, or internal bleeding. In pregnant women, severe abdominal pain can also signal a serious pregnancy-related complication. Act now: Go to the nearest hospital or call emergency services immediately. Avoid eating, drinking, or taking pain medicine until a doctor has assessed the situation, as this can make diagnosis more difficult. 7.

7. Loss of Consciousness
Fainting that does not resolve quickly, being unresponsive to voice or touch, or any period where a person cannot be woken up are medical emergencies. Loss of consciousness can be caused by a heart problem, a severe drop in blood sugar, a stroke, a serious head injury, severe blood loss, or a seizure, several of which require urgent treatment to prevent permanent harm. Act now: Call emergency services immediately. While waiting for help, keep the person lying on their side if they are breathing, and do not put anything in their mouth. General Safety Reminders
Do not wait for symptoms to "get worse" before seeking help; for the conditions listed above, acting early gives the best chance of a full recovery.

Do not rely on home remedies, rest, or over-the-counter medicine alone when any of these warning signs are present. If you are unsure whether a situation is a true emergency, it is safer to seek immediate medical care than to wait and assume it will pass. Keep the nearest hospital's location and your local emergency ambulance number easily accessible for yourself and your family. If you are with someone showing these symptoms, stay with them, keep them as calm and comfortable as possible, and get them to care as quickly and safely as you can. Source Basis

FEVER — MYTH VS FACT
Common Misunderstandings About Fever and Its Management
Introduction
Fever is one of the most common reasons people, especially parents of young children, seek medical advice or worry at home. Along with genuine concern comes a great deal of confusion, passed down through habit, word of mouth, or well-meaning but inaccurate advice. This document addresses some of the most common myths about fever and offers simple, factual clarifications to support better understanding and calmer, more informed care at home. Myth 1: Fever itself is a dangerous illness that must be brought down immediately. Fact: Fever is not a disease — it is the body's natural defence response, helping the immune system fight infection.

In most cases, the underlying cause of the fever matters far more than the number on the thermometer, and mild fevers often don't need urgent medication. Myth 2: A higher fever always means a more serious illness. Fact: The height of a fever does not reliably indicate how serious the illness is. A person can have a mild infection with a high temperature, or a more serious one with only a low-grade fever, so other symptoms and overall condition matter more than the exact reading. Myth 3: You should cover a feverish person with heavy blankets or clothes to “sweat it out.”
Fact: Bundling up traps heat and can push the body's temperature higher, adding to discomfort. It is generally better to dress the person in light, breathable clothing and keep the room comfortably ventilated.

Myth 4: Sponging with ice-cold water or alcohol is the fastest way to cool a fever. Fact: Ice-cold water or alcohol rubs can cause shivering, which may raise body temperature further, and alcohol can be absorbed through the skin, especially in children. Lukewarm sponging, rest, and adequate fluids are the commonly recommended supportive measures instead. Myth 5: If a fever doesn't come down with medicine, the illness must be serious. Fact: How a fever responds to fever-reducing medicine does not reliably indicate how serious the underlying illness is. Some infections cause fevers that are simply slower to settle, so this alone is not a reason for panic, though a fever lasting several days should still be checked by a doctor. Myth 6: Every fever needs to be treated with an antibiotic.

Myth 6: Every fever needs to be treated with an antibiotic. Fact: Most fevers are caused by viral infections, which do not respond to antibiotics at all. Taking antibiotics unnecessarily does not help recovery and can contribute to antibiotic resistance, so a doctor should decide if and when antibiotics are actually needed. Myth 7: High fever always causes brain damage or fits in children. Fact: The brain has a built-in thermostat that generally keeps infection-related fever within a limited range, and brain damage from fever alone is rare. Some young children can experience febrile seizures with rapid temperature changes, which are frightening but usually brief and without lasting harm; even so, a doctor should always be consulted after one.

Myth 8: Skipping food while feverish helps the body recover faster. Fact: The body needs energy and fluids to fight infection, so light, easily digestible food and plenty of fluids like water, ORS, soup, or buttermilk are generally recommended during fever. Prolonged fasting can lead to weakness and dehydration, which may slow recovery. Myth 9: In dengue or suspected viral fever, any fever-reducing medicine can be used, including common painkillers. Fact: Certain common painkillers, such as ibuprofen and aspirin, are best avoided in suspected dengue or similar illnesses because they can increase bleeding risk. Public health guidance generally recommends paracetamol for fever relief in these situations, and a doctor should confirm the diagnosis and appropriate medicine.

Myth 10: Once the fever goes away for a few hours, the illness is over and treatment can stop. Fact: A temporary drop in temperature does not always mean the infection is fully resolved, and fever can return as medication wears off or if the underlying illness is still active. It's important to complete the course of care advised by a health worker and to keep watching for warning symptoms even after the fever seems to settle.

A Note on When to Seek Medical Care
While many fevers can be safely observed and managed at home with rest and fluids, a doctor or nearest health facility should be consulted if the fever is very high, lasts more than two to three days, is accompanied by symptoms such as difficulty breathing, repeated vomiting, unusual drowsiness, rash, bleeding, seizures, or if the person is a very young infant, elderly, pregnant, or has an existing health condition. When in doubt, it is always safer to seek a professional opinion rather than rely on assumptions. Source Basis

First Aid for Suspected Fractures
Immediate Care Before Medical Help Arrives
A fracture is a broken or cracked bone, most often caused by a fall, accident, sports injury, or direct blow. Fractures can range from a small hairline crack to a bone that has broken through the skin. Any suspected fracture needs professional medical evaluation. The goal of first aid is not to treat the fracture itself, but to keep the injured person safe, prevent further damage, and support them until trained medical help takes over. What to Do Immediately
1. Stay calm and keep the injured person calm. Reassure them and encourage them to stay still, since anxiety and movement can make the injury worse. 2. Check for danger first.

2. Check for danger first. Make sure the surroundings are safe before approaching, and do not move the person unless they are in immediate danger (such as fire, traffic, or floodwater). 3. Keep the injured part still. Support the limb or area gently in the position you found it, using your hands, a rolled towel, or cushions to prevent movement. 4. Control any bleeding. If there is a wound, apply gentle, firm pressure around it (not directly on a protruding bone) using a clean cloth or sterile dressing. 5. Immobilize only if trained and help is delayed. A firm object such as a folded newspaper, magazine, or board can be placed alongside the limb and secured loosely with cloth strips, padded so it does not press directly on the skin. 6. Apply a cold pack if available.

6. Apply a cold pack if available. Wrap ice or a cold pack in a cloth (never place it directly on skin) and hold it near, not on, the injury site for short periods to reduce swelling and pain. 7. Watch for shock. If the person looks pale, feels faint, or is breathing rapidly, help them lie down, keep them warm, and if there is no suspected spinal, head, or leg injury, raise their legs slightly. 8. Monitor breathing and responsiveness continuously until emergency responders arrive, and be ready to describe what happened and what care has already been given. What NOT to Do
• Do not try to straighten, realign, or push a bent limb or a bone back into place, even if it looks deformed. • Do not push a bone that is sticking out of the skin back in, and do not touch or probe an open wound.

• Do not move the person unnecessarily, especially if a neck, back, hip, or thigh injury is suspected, as improper movement can cause serious additional harm. • Do not let the injured person walk on or use the injured limb, even if they insist they can manage. • Do not apply ice directly to bare skin, as this can cause cold burns. • Do not give food, water, or medication by mouth, in case surgery or anesthesia is needed soon after. • Do not attempt a splint if you are not trained and help is only minutes away; an incorrectly applied splint can restrict blood flow or worsen the injury. • Do not ignore signs of numbness, tingling, or a cold, pale limb below the injury, as this suggests blood flow or nerve involvement that needs urgent attention.

When to Call Emergency Services
Call an ambulance (108 in India, or the local emergency number) immediately if any of the following apply:
• The bone has broken through the skin, or there is heavy or uncontrolled bleeding. • A fracture of the skull, spine, neck, hip, pelvis, or thigh bone is suspected. • The injured person is unconscious, unresponsive, or not breathing normally. • There is visible deformity, or the limb appears at an unnatural angle. • The person shows signs of shock: pale or clammy skin, rapid breathing, dizziness, or confusion. • The area beyond the injury (fingers or toes) becomes numb, cold, or discolored. • The injury resulted from a major fall, road accident, or high-impact trauma.

• The injury resulted from a major fall, road accident, or high-impact trauma. • You are unsure of the severity, since it is always safer to seek professional evaluation for a suspected fracture. Source Basis

Heat Stroke: Recognizing and Responding Immediately
Health Awareness Reference — General Public Guidance for Odisha's Summer Season
Odisha regularly experiences severe heatwave conditions between April and June, with high humidity adding to the risk. Heat stroke is the most dangerous heat-related illness and is a medical emergency — the body's temperature-control system fails, and body temperature can rise to dangerous levels within a short time. Warning signs include hot, dry, flushed skin with little or no sweating, confusion or agitation, slurred speech, dizziness, a very fast heartbeat, seizures, and loss of consciousness. Recognizing these signs early and acting immediately can save a life. What to Do Immediately
Act immediately.

Act immediately. If you suspect heat stroke, treat it as a medical emergency from the very first sign — do not wait to see if symptoms worsen. Move the person to a cool place right away. Move the person out of the sun into shade, a ventilated room, or any cooler space, and keep others from crowding around them. Remove excess clothing. Take off heavy outer clothing so heat can escape from the body; light clothing can remain. Begin active cooling without delay. Douse or sponge the person with cool (not ice-cold) water, or use wet cloths and towels over the body, re-wetting them frequently. Fanning the person while the skin is wet speeds up cooling. Apply cold packs to key areas.

Place ice packs or cold, wet cloths on the neck, armpits, and groin, where blood vessels are close to the skin, to help lower body temperature faster. Monitor temperature if possible. If a thermometer is available, monitor the person's temperature and continue cooling until it drops to a safer level; stop aggressive cooling once the person is stable, to avoid overcooling. Keep the person positioned comfortably. Have the person lie down with the head and shoulders slightly raised. Give small sips of water only if the person is fully conscious. If the person is conscious, alert, and not vomiting, offer small sips of plain cool water. Do not force fluids. Call for emergency help immediately.

Overview
Good hygiene, safe drinking water, and proper sanitation are among the simplest and most powerful ways to protect health. Many common illnesses, especially diarrhoea, typhoid, cholera, worm infections, and skin and eye infections, spread because of dirty hands, unsafe water, or poor sanitation. These illnesses are largely preventable. Simple daily habits, such as washing hands at the right times, drinking clean water, and using a toilet instead of open defecation, can greatly reduce sickness in a household and community.

Good hygiene is especially important for protecting young children, pregnant women, and elderly family members, who are more vulnerable to infections. This document explains the key daily practices that support health, why they matter, and how government programmes are helping communities in Odisha and across India access safe water and sanitation.

Key Practices
Handwashing
Wash hands with soap and clean water before eating or preparing food
Wash hands after using the toilet
Wash hands after cleaning a child, changing a baby, or handling waste
Wash hands before feeding a baby or young child
Rub soap on both sides of the hands, between fingers, and under nails for at least 20 seconds, then rinse with clean water
If soap is not available, ash or clean sand can be used, followed by rinsing with water
Safe Drinking Water
Drink water only from a safe, protected source, such as a treated tap connection, protected borewell, or covered well
Store drinking water in a clean, covered container, and use a clean cup or ladle to draw water rather than dipping hands inside
If the safety of water is uncertain, boil it before drinking, or use a household water filter or purification method recommended by local health workers
Keep drinking water separate from water used for washing or other household purposes
Clean water storage containers regularly to prevent contamination
Sanitation
Always use a toilet instead of defecating in the open, for both adults and children
Keep toilets clean and in good repair, with water available for use after each visit
Dispose of household waste and garbage properly, away from drinking water sources
Keep the area around the home, especially around water sources, free from stagnant water and waste, as these attract mosquitoes and other disease-carrying insects
Wash fruits and vegetables with clean water before eating or cooking
Cover food to protect it from flies and dust

Diseases such as diarrhoea, typhoid, hepatitis A, and cholera spread mainly through dirty hands, contaminated water, and unsafe sanitation.

Washing hands with soap at key times can significantly reduce the spread of diarrhoeal and respiratory illnesses, both of which remain leading causes of sickness, especially in young children. Unsafe water and poor sanitation also contribute to worm infections, which can affect children's growth, nutrition, and school attendance. Skin infections and eye infections such as trachoma are also linked to poor hygiene and limited access to clean water. When communities have access to safe water, functioning toilets, and good hygiene habits, rates of illness fall, children stay healthier and attend school more regularly, and healthcare costs for families are reduced. Good hygiene during childbirth and in the days after also protects the health of mothers and newborns.

Understanding High Blood Pressure
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base | General Public Information Only
Overview
High blood pressure, also called hypertension, is a condition where the force of blood pushing against the walls of the blood vessels stays too high over time. Blood pressure is written as two numbers, such as 120/80. The first (higher) number is the pressure when the heart beats, and the second (lower) number is the pressure when the heart rests between beats. A blood pressure reading of 140/90 or higher, checked on more than one occasion, is generally considered high.

Blood pressure naturally rises and falls during the day depending on activity, emotion, and rest, but when it stays high most of the time, it can slowly damage the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes. High blood pressure is often called a 'silent' condition because most people do not feel unwell even when their blood pressure is high. It is very common across India, in both cities and villages, and its numbers are rising. The only reliable way to know if a person has high blood pressure is to get it checked with a blood pressure machine. Common Symptoms
Most people with high blood pressure do not notice any symptoms at all, which is why regular checking is so important.

When symptoms do appear, they are often signs that blood pressure has become very high, and may include:
Headache, especially at the back of the head
Dizziness or a spinning sensation
Blurred or disturbed eyesight
Chest discomfort or a feeling of heaviness
Shortness of breath
Nosebleeds that are unusual or hard to stop
A fast or irregular heartbeat
Unusual tiredness or fatigue
Since high blood pressure usually has no warning signs, it is often found only during a routine health check. Regular blood pressure checks, even when a person feels completely well, are the best way to detect it early.

Causes
High blood pressure often develops because of a combination of habits, body factors, and family background:
Eating too much salt, or regularly eating salty, packaged, or pickled foods
Low intake of fruits and vegetables
Being overweight or having extra fat around the stomach
Low levels of physical activity
Use of tobacco (smoking or chewing) and regular alcohol use
Long-term stress and poor sleep
Family history of high blood pressure
Increasing age, especially after 40 years
Existing health conditions such as diabetes or kidney disease
Exposure to air pollution over long periods
In most people, several of these factors act together over time. This is why lifestyle habits play such a large role in both preventing and managing high blood pressure.

When to See a Doctor
Every adult should get their blood pressure checked regularly, even without any symptoms, since high blood pressure often has no warning signs.

In addition, the following signs point to a possible emergency and need urgent medical attention without delay:
Severe headache that comes on suddenly and does not go away
Chest pain, tightness, or pressure
Difficulty breathing or severe shortness of breath
Sudden weakness, numbness, or drooping on one side of the face or body
Slurred speech or trouble speaking or understanding others
Sudden blurred vision, double vision, or loss of vision
Confusion, difficulty staying awake, or fainting
Severe nosebleed that will not stop
Very high blood pressure reading along with any of the above symptoms
High blood pressure discovered or suspected during pregnancy, especially with swelling of hands or face
If any of these red-flag signs appear, the person should be taken to the nearest hospital or Primary Health Centre (PHC) immediately, as they could indicate a heart attack, stroke, or other emergency.

Every hour matters in these situations. Home Care and Prevention
High blood pressure can often be prevented or kept under control through simple, everyday lifestyle habits.

These habits also support people already living with high blood pressure:
Healthy Eating
Reduce salt intake; avoid adding extra salt at the table and limit pickles, papad, and salty snacks
Eat more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains such as unpolished rice or millets
Limit fried, oily, and processed packaged foods
Choose fresh, home-cooked food over ready-made or restaurant food when possible
Drink enough water through the day
Staying Active
Aim for at least 30 minutes of walking or moderate physical activity most days of the week
Everyday activities such as farm work, walking, or household chores also help
Avoid long periods of sitting without moving
Healthy Habits
Maintain a healthy body weight
Avoid tobacco in all forms and limit alcohol consumption
Manage stress through rest, family time, prayer, or community activities
Aim for regular, adequate sleep each night
General Care Awareness
Get blood pressure checked regularly, especially after age 40 or with a family history of hypertension
Keep a simple record of blood pressure readings if checked often
Attend follow-up check-ups at the local health centre as advised
If feeling unwell, rest, drink fluids, and consult a doctor rather than self-treating
This document does not cover medicines or treatment plans.

Any decisions about medication, dosage, or treatment must be made only by a qualified doctor. Odisha-Specific Notes

Free blood pressure screening is available at government health facilities, including Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres (PHCs), and Community Health Centres (CHCs), under national and state NCD control programmes

Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY)
India's Maternal Health Cash Assistance Scheme, Explained Simply
A Public Awareness Reference Guide
1. Overview
Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) is a safe motherhood scheme run by the Government of India under the National Health Mission (NHM). It was launched in April 2005 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The scheme's main goal is to reduce deaths of mothers and newborns by encouraging pregnant women to deliver their babies in a hospital or health centre, with the help of trained doctors and nurses, instead of at home without medical support. JSY does this by providing cash assistance directly to the mother when she delivers at a government hospital or an accredited private health facility.

It also involves ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) workers, who guide and support pregnant women through pregnancy check-ups, the delivery itself, and care afterward. JSY is implemented in every state and union territory, with extra focus on states that have historically had lower rates of hospital deliveries, known as Low Performing States (LPS). 2. Eligibility
Eligibility under JSY depends partly on where a woman lives and, in some cases, on her economic background:
In Low Performing States, all pregnant women delivering in a government or accredited private health facility are eligible for cash assistance, regardless of their age or how many children they already have.

In High Performing States, women from Below Poverty Line (BPL) households, and women belonging to Scheduled Castes (SC) or Scheduled Tribes (ST), are eligible for cash assistance for institutional delivery, generally up to two live births. BPL pregnant women who prefer to deliver at home, rather than at a health facility, are also entitled to a smaller cash assistance, regardless of age or number of children. Women choosing to deliver at an accredited private hospital are usually required to show valid BPL, SC, or ST proof, along with a referral from the ASHA worker, ANM, or medical officer.

Because eligibility rules can vary slightly depending on the state's classification and local guidelines, pregnant women and their families should confirm current criteria with their nearest ASHA worker, ANM, or health centre. 3. Benefits
JSY combines a cash incentive with supportive care during pregnancy, delivery, and after childbirth:
Cash Assistance for Institutional Delivery
* Low Performing States generally include states that have historically had lower institutional delivery rates; all other states and union territories are classified as High Performing States. Actual classification and amounts may be revised over time. Other Benefits
A separate incentive is paid to the ASHA worker for accompanying and supporting the mother through antenatal check-ups and institutional delivery.

At least a minimum number of free antenatal check-ups are provided before delivery, along with a Mother and Child Protection Card and a JSY card to track entitlements. JSY is closely linked with the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), which provides free delivery, free medicines, free diagnostic tests, free diet during the hospital stay, and free transport to and from the health facility, at no cost to the mother. Cash assistance is generally transferred directly into the mother's bank account, so beneficiaries are encouraged to open a bank account, including through schemes like the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, if they do not already have one. 4.

4. How to Apply
As soon as pregnancy is confirmed, register with the nearest Anganwadi Centre, Sub-Centre, or Primary Health Centre (PHC), ideally within the first few months. The local ASHA worker can help with this registration. Complete the recommended antenatal check-ups and collect the Mother and Child Protection Card and JSY card issued by the ANM or ASHA worker; these track eligibility and entitlements through the pregnancy. Provide bank account details and required identity documents, such as Aadhaar, so that the cash assistance can be transferred directly once the delivery is complete. At the time of delivery, go to a government health facility or an accredited private hospital; the ASHA worker can help arrange transport and accompany the mother.

After delivery, ensure discharge documents and the JSY card are submitted at the health facility so that the cash assistance can be processed and credited to the bank account. Families without easy access to these facilities, or with questions about their entitlement, can reach out to their ASHA worker, the nearest PHC or Sub-Centre, or call the NHM toll-free health helpline for guidance. 5. Jaundice (Hepatitis A and E): A Public Health Reference
Health Awareness Chatbot Knowledge Base
Overview
Jaundice is not a disease by itself. It is a sign that shows up when the liver is not working properly, causing the skin and the white part of the eyes to turn yellow. In India, one of the most common causes of sudden jaundice, especially in children and young adults, is a viral infection of the liver called hepatitis. Hepatitis A and hepatitis E are two types of liver infection that spread mainly through dirty water or contaminated food. Both illnesses are usually short-term and most people recover fully with rest and care at home. However, in some cases, especially in pregnant women, hepatitis E can become serious and needs urgent medical attention.

Because these infections spread easily in areas with unsafe drinking water and poor sanitation, they are common in many rural and semi-urban parts of India, including Odisha. Common Symptoms
Symptoms usually appear a few weeks after a person is exposed to the virus. Not everyone shows every symptom, and young children may have very mild or no symptoms at all. Common signs include:
Yellowing of the eyes and skin (jaundice)
Dark-coloured urine and pale or clay-coloured stools
Tiredness and weakness
Loss of appetite
Nausea and vomiting
Mild fever
Pain or discomfort in the upper right side of the stomach, near the liver
Joint pain (in some cases)
Most people feel unwell for one to a few weeks, and the illness usually goes away on its own within a few weeks to a couple of months.

Causes
Hepatitis A and hepatitis E viruses spread mainly through the faecal-oral route. This means the virus leaves the body of an infected person through stool and enters another person's body through the mouth, usually because of unsafe water or food. Common causes include:
Drinking water that has been contaminated with sewage or human waste
Eating food that was washed, cooked, or handled with unclean water or unwashed hands
Eating raw or undercooked food, including fruits and vegetables washed in unsafe water
Poor toilet and sanitation facilities that allow waste to mix with water sources
Living in crowded conditions with poor hygiene practices
These viruses are not usually spread by casual contact such as talking, hugging, or sitting near an infected person.

The main route of spread is through what people eat and drink. When to See a Doctor (Red Flags)
While most cases of hepatitis A and E are mild, some signs mean the illness may be getting serious and need urgent medical attention.

A doctor or health centre should be consulted immediately if a person has:
Yellowing of the eyes or skin that is getting worse quickly
Repeated vomiting, unable to keep fluids down
Severe weakness, confusion, or unusual drowsiness
Little or no urine, or urine that is very dark
Swelling of the stomach, legs, or feet
Bleeding or unusual bruising from the gums, nose, or skin
High fever that does not go down
Severe pain in the upper stomach
Any jaundice symptom in a pregnant woman, at any stage of pregnancy
Jaundice in a small child, an elderly person, or someone with an existing liver illness
Pregnant women need extra caution. Hepatitis E can be dangerous during pregnancy, particularly in the later months, and can lead to serious complications for both mother and baby.
Any pregnant woman with jaundice symptoms should be taken to a health facility without delay.

Any pregnant woman with jaundice symptoms should be taken to a health facility without delay. Home Care and Prevention
General care during recovery
Take plenty of rest and avoid heavy physical work until fully recovered
Drink enough clean, safe fluids to avoid dehydration
Eat light, easily digestible meals; avoid oily and heavy food
Avoid alcohol completely, as it puts extra strain on the liver
Do not take any medicine without a doctor's advice, since some medicines can affect the liver
Follow up with a health worker or doctor to check on recovery
Preventing hepatitis A and E
Drink only boiled, filtered, or otherwise safely treated water
Wash hands with soap and water before eating, before cooking, and after using the toilet
Use a clean toilet and avoid open defecation
Wash fruits and vegetables properly with safe water before eating
Eat freshly cooked, hot food and avoid food from unhygienic sources
Keep drinking water storage containers covered and clean
Ask a doctor or local health worker about the hepatitis A vaccine, especially for children
Community-level steps, such as protecting water sources from sewage contamination and improving sanitation, play a major role in preventing outbreaks.

Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha has seen repeated outbreaks of jaundice linked to hepatitis A and E, and unsafe drinking water has consistently been identified as the main cause. A well-documented outbreak in Sambalpur district and nearby areas involved thousands of cases and several deaths, traced back to contamination of the public water supply. Investigations into other outbreaks in the state, including in Bhubaneswar, have found that bore wells located near open sewage or drains were the source of infection. Studies of rural Odisha villages have also found frequent faecal contamination of ponds, groundwater sources, and stored household water, particularly during and after the monsoon season.

For rural communities in Odisha, the following points are especially important:
Flooding and heavy monsoon rains can contaminate wells, ponds, and pipelines, so extra care with water safety is needed during and after the rainy season
Water pipelines that run close to drains or sewage lines are a known risk; leaking or damaged pipes should be reported to local authorities
Bore wells and hand pumps near open defecation areas or soak pits should be avoided for drinking water where possible
Boiling water or using safe household treatment (such as proper chlorination or filtration) before drinking is strongly advised in areas without a reliable safe piped supply
Any sudden increase in jaundice cases in a village or locality should be reported promptly to the nearest health sub-centre or Anganwadi worker, as early reporting helps contain outbreaks
Government programmes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission aim to provide safe piped drinking water to rural households, and community participation in maintaining clean water sources remains an important part of preventing hepatitis outbreaks in the state.
