Family Planning: A General Awareness Guide
Overview
Family planning refers to the ability of individuals and couples to decide, of their own free will, the number of children they wish to have and the spacing between births. It is achieved through access to accurate information, counselling, and a range of contraceptive methods, along with care for couples experiencing infertility. Family planning is recognized globally as an important part of reproductive health and is closely linked to the wellbeing of mothers, children, and families.

This document provides general awareness information; it does not recommend any specific method, and personal decisions about family planning should always be made in consultation with a qualified healthcare provider based on individual health and circumstances. Key Facts
Family planning allows couples to plan pregnancies according to their own wishes and circumstances, supporting the health of mothers and children and contributing to family wellbeing. A range of contraceptive methods exist, broadly grouped as temporary (reversible) methods, such as condoms, oral contraceptive pills, injectables, and intrauterine devices, and permanent methods, such as male or female sterilization.

Only condoms offer dual protection, helping to prevent both unintended pregnancy and the transmission of sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Choosing a suitable method depends on personal health, life stage, future plans for children, and individual preference, and is best done in consultation with a healthcare provider. Access to family planning is considered a part of reproductive rights, supporting individuals' ability to make informed and voluntary choices about their reproductive health. In India, family planning services, including counselling and a range of contraceptive options, are made available through the public health system, generally free of cost or at a subsidized rate.

Government health workers, including ASHAs (Accredited Social Health Activists) and ANMs (Auxiliary Nurse Midwives), play an important role in providing information, counselling, and doorstep access to certain contraceptive methods in many parts of the country. Common Concerns
Individuals and couples often have questions or hesitations related to family planning. Some common concerns include:
Side effects: Some contraceptive methods can cause temporary side effects, such as changes in menstrual patterns or mild discomfort. Discussing these possibilities with a healthcare provider beforehand can help set realistic expectations and address concerns quickly if they arise.

Myths and misinformation: Various misconceptions exist about contraception, such as beliefs that certain methods cause permanent infertility or are unsafe for young or unmarried individuals. Reliable information from a qualified healthcare provider, rather than informal sources, is the best way to address such concerns. Social or family pressure: In many communities, decisions about family size or contraception can be influenced by family expectations or social norms. Family planning is intended to be a voluntary and informed choice for the individuals or couple concerned, made without coercion. Access and affordability: Some individuals, particularly in rural or underserved areas, may face challenges accessing contraceptive services or products.

Public health programs aim to improve access through community health workers, government facilities, and subsidized supplies. Privacy and stigma: Some people feel hesitant to seek family planning services due to privacy concerns or social stigma, especially younger or unmarried individuals. Health facilities are expected to provide confidential and respectful services to all clients regardless of age or marital status. When to Seek Medical Advice
It is advisable to consult a doctor, ASHA worker, ANM, or nearby health facility in situations such as:
Before starting any contraceptive method, to discuss suitability based on personal health history and needs. If experiencing side effects that are severe, persistent, or concerning after starting a contraceptive method.

If there is a suspected method failure, such as a missed pill or condom breakage, particularly regarding options like emergency contraception. When planning a pregnancy, to discuss preconception health and appropriate timing. If facing difficulty conceiving after a reasonable period of trying, which may warrant evaluation for infertility. For guidance on switching from one contraceptive method to another, or on resuming fertility after using a long-term method. A visit to the nearest Primary Health Centre (PHC), Community Health Centre (CHC), or a conversation with a local ASHA or ANM is a good starting point for personalized guidance.

Odisha has also promoted the doorstep delivery of contraceptives such as condoms and oral pills through ASHA workers, extended to all districts of the state, to improve access, particularly in rural areas.

Couples in Odisha can approach their local ASHA, ANM, Sub-Centre, Primary Health Centre, or Community Health Centre for information and services related to family planning, including counselling on the range of available methods. Source Basis

Menstrual Hygiene: An Awareness Guide
Overview
Menstruation is a normal, healthy biological process experienced by girls and women, typically beginning between ages 10 and 15 and continuing on a monthly basis until menopause. Practicing good menstrual hygiene helps prevent infections, supports comfort and confidence, and allows girls and women to continue their daily activities, including school and work, without disruption. Understanding the facts about menstruation and addressing it openly within families and communities helps reduce stigma and supports better health outcomes for adolescent girls and women. Key Facts
A normal menstrual cycle usually lasts around 21 to 35 days, with bleeding typically lasting 3 to 7 days, though this can vary from person to person.

Using a clean absorbent material, such as a sanitary napkin, cloth pad, tampon, or menstrual cup, and changing it regularly (generally every 4 to 6 hours or as needed) helps maintain hygiene and reduce the risk of infection. Washing the genital area with clean water, and soap if available, during menstruation is recommended; harsh or scented products are generally unnecessary and can sometimes cause irritation. Hands should be washed with soap before and after changing a menstrual product. Used sanitary products should be disposed of properly, ideally wrapped and placed in a covered bin, and not flushed down toilets, to support hygienic and environmentally responsible waste management.

There is no medical restriction on bathing, exercising, or carrying out most daily activities during menstruation; in fact, staying active can help ease period-related discomfort for many people. Menstrual health and hygiene is recognized by national and global public health bodies as an important part of adolescent health, gender equity, and overall well-being, not merely a private or hidden matter. Common Concerns
Many adolescent girls and their families have questions or worries related to menstruation. Some common concerns include:
Irregular periods: It is common for cycles to be somewhat irregular in the first one to two years after menstruation begins, as the body's hormonal patterns are still stabilizing.

Persistent or very irregular cycles beyond this period are worth discussing with a healthcare provider. Pain or cramps: Mild to moderate cramping during periods is common and can often be managed with rest, a warm compress, light activity, and over-the-counter pain relief if recommended by a doctor or pharmacist. Severe pain that interferes with daily life should be evaluated by a healthcare professional. Heavy or prolonged bleeding: While flow varies between individuals, unusually heavy bleeding (needing to change protection very frequently) or periods lasting much longer than a week may indicate an underlying condition that should be checked by a doctor.

Myths and social restrictions: In many communities, menstruating girls and women face restrictions around cooking, entering religious spaces, or social participation. These practices are cultural rather than medical, and menstruation does not make a person unclean or make it unsafe for them to carry out ordinary activities. Access to products: Cost or availability of sanitary products can be a genuine barrier for some families. Government-supported and community programs in several states aim to improve access to affordable menstrual products, particularly for school-going adolescent girls.

When to Seek Medical Advice
While most menstrual experiences are normal, it is advisable to consult a doctor or health worker if any of the following occur:
Periods have not started by around age 15–16, or there is a sudden, unexplained stop in periods after they have been regular. Bleeding is extremely heavy, requires changing protection more than every 1–2 hours, or includes large clots. Periods last significantly longer than 7 days on a regular basis. Severe pain that does not improve with rest or usual pain relief, or that interferes with daily activities. Unusual vaginal discharge, itching, strong odour, or fever alongside menstrual symptoms, which may indicate infection. Bleeding between periods or after any long gap since the last period, when not expected.

Bleeding between periods or after any long gap since the last period, when not expected. A local Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA), Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM), Anganwadi worker, school health counsellor, or nearby Primary Health Centre (PHC) can be a good first point of contact for guidance and referral. Nutrition Myths vs Facts
Nutrition is central to good health, but everyday conversations in Indian households are often filled with food-related beliefs that mix tradition with misinformation. This reference document addresses some common nutrition myths with clear, simple facts to help families make informed, balanced dietary choices. Myth: Eating fat, like ghee or oil, is the main reason people gain weight and should be avoided completely. Fact: Fats are an essential part of a balanced diet and help the body absorb certain vitamins, but the type and amount matter.

Guidance from Indian nutrition experts encourages moderate use of healthy fats such as those from nuts, seeds, and cooking oils, rather than eliminating fat altogether, while keeping overall calorie intake and physical activity in balance. Myth: Rice and roti are unhealthy and should be cut out completely to avoid diabetes. Fact: Cereals like rice and wheat are a traditional part of Indian meals and can be included as part of a balanced diet. The concern raised by health experts is more about the overall proportion of the plate coming from refined carbohydrates and about pairing cereals with adequate protein, vegetables, and pulses, rather than needing to eliminate them entirely. Myth: Skipping meals, especially breakfast, helps with weight loss.

Myth: Skipping meals, especially breakfast, helps with weight loss. Fact: Skipping meals often leads to overeating later in the day and can affect energy levels and concentration. Regular, balanced meals spread through the day are generally recommended for maintaining steady energy and supporting healthy metabolism. Myth: All carbohydrates are bad and should be avoided for good health. Fact: Carbohydrates are the body's primary source of energy, and whole grains, pulses, fruits, and vegetables provide carbohydrates along with fibre and important nutrients. The distinction health guidelines emphasize is between minimally processed, fibre-rich carbohydrate sources and heavily refined ones like white sugar and refined flour, rather than avoiding carbohydrates as a whole.

Myth: Protein is only needed by bodybuilders or athletes, not by ordinary people. Fact: Protein is necessary for everyone, as it supports muscle maintenance, immune function, and overall growth and repair of body tissues. Many Indian diets tend to be lower in protein relative to overall calorie intake, so including pulses, dairy, eggs, or other protein-rich foods according to one's dietary preferences is encouraged for people of all activity levels. Myth: Fruits are unhealthy for people with diabetes and should be completely avoided. Fact: Whole fruits contain fibre, vitamins, and natural sugars that are generally absorbed more slowly than sugars in processed foods or juices.

People with diabetes are usually advised to enjoy fruit in sensible portions as part of an overall balanced meal plan, ideally guided by their doctor or dietitian, rather than cutting it out completely. Myth: Homemade or natural remedies like herbal powders or detox drinks can replace medical treatment for nutrition-related conditions. Fact: While a variety of traditional foods can be part of a healthy diet, they are not a substitute for medical evaluation and treatment of diagnosed conditions such as anaemia, diabetes, or malnutrition. Public health guidance recommends consulting a healthcare provider for proper diagnosis and treatment alongside dietary improvements. Myth: Packaged foods labelled 'natural,' 'healthy,' or 'no added sugar' are always a good dietary choice.

Fact: Food labels can sometimes be misleading, and a product can carry such claims while still containing significant amounts of salt, saturated fat, or hidden sugars. Reading the ingredient list and nutrition information on the label carefully is a better way to judge a packaged food's healthiness than relying on marketing claims alone. Myth: Curd or milk should never be consumed at night as it is always harmful. Fact: This belief is more rooted in traditional practice than in general medical evidence, and dairy products like curd and milk can be part of a healthy diet at various times of day for most people. Those with specific digestive sensitivities or conditions may wish to seek personalized advice from a doctor or dietitian.

Myth: A drastic or extreme diet is the fastest and best way to lose weight and get healthy. Fact: Sudden, extreme dietary changes are often difficult to sustain and can lead to nutrient deficiencies or a rebound in weight once normal eating resumes. Gradual, balanced changes that include a variety of food groups, controlled portions, and regular physical activity are more consistent with general public health recommendations for long-term health. Public Health Awareness FAQ
 A friendly reference guide answering common health questions. Please remember this is general guidance, not a diagnosis. 1. What should I do if I have a fever? A fever usually means your body is working hard to fight off an infection, so try not to panic. Rest as much as you can, and drink plenty of fluids such as water, coconut water, or diluted juices to stay hydrated. Wear light, breathable clothing and you can sponge your body with lukewarm water to help you feel more comfortable. If the fever crosses 102°F, lasts more than two to three days, or comes with other worrying symptoms like rash or breathlessness, please see a doctor rather than waiting it out. A pharmacist or doctor can guide you on safe medication if you need something to ease the discomfort. 2.

2. What is ORS and how do I make it? ORS stands for Oral Rehydration Solution, a simple mix that replaces the fluids and salts your body loses during vomiting, diarrhea, or heavy sweating. The easiest option is a ready-made ORS packet from any pharmacy — just dissolve it in the exact amount of clean, boiled, and cooled water mentioned on the packet. If a packet isn't handy, you can make a basic version at home by mixing six level teaspoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of salt into one litre of clean water. Sip it slowly throughout the day, especially after every loose motion or vomiting episode, rather than drinking it all at once. Always make a fresh batch each day and throw away any solution left over after 24 hours. 3. When should I visit a doctor versus manage a symptom at home?

3. When should I visit a doctor versus manage a symptom at home? Mild symptoms like a light cold, slight headache, or low-grade fever can usually be managed at home with rest, fluids, and a little patience. However, you should see a doctor if a fever lasts more than two to three days, if you have trouble breathing, persistent vomiting, or signs of dehydration like reduced urination or dizziness. Severe pain, confusion, a rash that spreads quickly, or symptoms in a baby, elderly person, or pregnant woman also deserve prompt medical attention. When in doubt, it's always safer to get checked rather than wait, since early advice can prevent a small issue from becoming serious. Trust your instincts — if something feels off or isn't improving, reaching out to a healthcare provider is the right call. 4.

4. How can I prevent dengue and malaria? Both dengue and malaria spread through mosquito bites, so the best prevention is stopping mosquitoes from breeding and biting in the first place. Empty out any standing water around your home — in flower pots, coolers, tyres, or containers — since this is where mosquitoes lay eggs. Use mosquito nets while sleeping, apply mosquito repellent, and wear full-sleeved clothing, especially during early morning and evening hours when mosquitoes are most active. Installing screens on windows and doors and keeping your surroundings clean also helps a lot. Community efforts, like clearing garbage and covering water storage tanks, make a real difference in reducing mosquito populations for everyone. 5. What are the symptoms of common illnesses like malaria and typhoid?

5. What are the symptoms of common illnesses like malaria and typhoid? Malaria often shows up as high fever with chills and sweating, along with headache, body aches, and tiredness, sometimes following a cyclical pattern of fever and relief. Typhoid tends to cause a prolonged fever that gradually rises, along with weakness, stomach pain, poor appetite, and occasionally a mild rash. Because these symptoms can overlap with many other illnesses, it isn't possible or safe to self-diagnose based on symptoms alone. If you notice a persistent fever along with any of these signs, please visit a health facility for proper testing and guidance. Getting tested early helps ensure you get the right care quickly and avoid complications. 6. How do I check my eligibility for government health schemes?

6. How do I check my eligibility for government health schemes? Many government health schemes, such as Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY), offer free or subsidised treatment to eligible families, often based on income and socioeconomic criteria. You can check your eligibility through the official scheme website or mobile app by entering your details, such as your ration card or household ID. Your local ASHA worker, ANM, or the nearest Common Service Centre can also help you check and complete enrolment if you're unsure how to do it online. Many states also run a dedicated helpline number for scheme-related queries, which is a great option if you'd prefer to ask someone directly. Do keep your identity and address documents handy, as these are usually needed to confirm your eligibility. 7.

7. Where can I find my nearest health facility? Your nearest Primary Health Centre (PHC) or Community Health Centre (CHC) is usually the first place to go for common health concerns, and these are available in most areas. Your local ASHA or ANM worker is a great first point of contact — they know the area well and can guide you to the right facility. You can also check the National Health Mission or your state health department's website, which often have facility locators listing centres near you. In many regions, dialling a health helpline number like 104 or 108 can connect you to information about nearby facilities or emergency services. Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres are another good option, offering a range of basic services close to home.

Vaccine Myths vs Facts
A quick, reassuring guide separating common vaccine rumours from the facts. 1. Myth: Vaccines cause autism. Fact: This myth traces back to a single 1998 study that was later found to be seriously flawed and was retracted by the journal that published it. Since then, many large, independent studies across different countries have found no link between vaccines and autism. Health authorities worldwide, including the WHO, continue to affirm that vaccines are safe on this front. 2. Myth: Natural immunity from catching a disease is better than immunity from a vaccine. Fact: Vaccines train the immune system to recognise and fight a disease without exposing a person to the actual risks of that illness, such as severe complications or death.

Diseases like measles, polio, and rubella can cause serious harm or lifelong disability if caught naturally. Getting immunity through vaccination offers similar protection in a much safer way. 3. Myth: Giving several vaccines at the same visit overloads or weakens a child's immune system. Fact: A child's immune system deals with far more germs from everyday life, like a common cold, than it does from a combined set of vaccines. Receiving multiple vaccines together has not been shown to cause any negative effect on the body's defences. It also means fewer clinic visits and a better chance of completing the full schedule on time. 4. Myth: Vaccine side effects are usually dangerous.

4. Myth: Vaccine side effects are usually dangerous. Fact: Most people who get a vaccine experience only mild, short-lived effects, such as soreness at the injection site, slight fever, or tiredness, which typically go away within a day or two on their own. Serious reactions are extremely rare and are closely monitored by health authorities even after a vaccine is approved. Vaccines undergo rigorous testing before being introduced and continued safety monitoring afterward. 5. Myth: Diseases like measles and polio are basically gone, so vaccination isn't necessary anymore. Fact: These diseases became rare specifically because sustained, high vaccination coverage kept them under control, not because the germs disappeared.

When vaccination rates drop in a community, these diseases can and do return quickly, as seen in real outbreaks in various parts of the world. Continuing to vaccinate is what keeps these illnesses from making a comeback. 6. Myth: Vaccines contain harmful chemicals that poison the body. Fact: Vaccines do contain small amounts of ingredients like preservatives or adjuvants, but these are present in carefully studied, safe quantities and serve a purpose, such as keeping the vaccine sterile or improving how well it works. These ingredients have been extensively researched and are regularly reviewed by health and drug regulatory bodies. The amounts used are far too small to cause the harm that circulating rumours often suggest. 7. Myth: Vaccines can give you the disease they're meant to prevent.

7. Myth: Vaccines can give you the disease they're meant to prevent. Fact: Most vaccines use inactivated (killed) or partial versions of a germ, which cannot cause the disease itself. A few vaccines use a weakened live form of a germ, which in most people simply triggers a mild, harmless immune response rather than the actual illness. Any mild symptoms that occasionally follow vaccination, like slight fever, are a sign the body is building protection, not a sign of infection. 8. Myth: Vaccines affect fertility and cause infertility later in life. Fact: There is no credible scientific evidence linking any routine vaccine to infertility in men or women.

This particular myth has circulated widely on social media in various forms over the years and has been investigated and repeatedly disproven by health researchers and public health bodies. Vaccines are studied specifically for their effects on reproductive health as part of standard safety evaluation. 9. Myth: If most people around me are vaccinated, I don't need to get vaccinated myself. Fact: Community protection, often called herd immunity, only works when enough individuals are vaccinated, and it isn't a guarantee for any one unvaccinated person. Relying on others being vaccinated still leaves you personally at risk of catching the disease, especially while travelling or during local outbreaks.

Getting vaccinated protects you directly, in addition to helping protect those around you who may be too young or medically unable to be vaccinated themselves. Sources
